summary: This RFC extends IMAP4rev1 so that user names, mail addresses, and message headers can use UTF-8 encoded international characters. It replaces RFC 6855. It does not extend IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051), since that version already includes the needed support. This RFC obsoletes RFC 6855.

eli5.summary: Not every name is written with English letters. This lets email programs store and fetch messages with names and addresses in any language's letters.

questions: how does imap handle international email addresses
how does imap handle international email
subtitle: How IMAP servers and clients negotiate UTF-8 for mailbox names, quoted strings and internationalized message headers.

tldr.problem: IMAP4rev1 forbids 8-bit characters in atoms and quoted-strings, so user-visible names and message headers in non-ASCII scripts are awkward or impossible to handle directly.
tldr.mechanism: Servers advertise the UTF8=ACCEPT or UTF8=ONLY capability, and a client opts in with ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT, after which UTF-8 is allowed in quoted-strings, mailbox names and message headers.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 6855, drops the APPEND UTF8 data item to match IMAP4rev2, and does not extend IMAP4rev2 itself because that protocol already includes this support.

today: RFC 9755 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025. It obsoletes RFC 6855 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9755 is part of the Email Address Internationalization protocols. It extends IMAP4rev1 (RFC 3501) to permit UTF-8 in message headers, as described in RFC 6532, and adds a way to use UTF-8 for mailbox names. It creates two new IMAP capabilities that servers use to advertise the extension.

The RFC assumes the server runs in a fully internationalized environment, where every client can accept non-ASCII header fields. The document admits that this assumption is unrealistic in many environments, at least during a transition period, and Section 8 deals with that. It replaces an earlier experimental approach, RFC 5738, and also replaces RFC 6855.

It does not extend IMAP4rev2 (RFC 9051), since that protocol already includes everything in this extension.
sections.eli5: Email uses an old rule that only plain letters are allowed in some places. This document allows letters from every language, if both sides agree to it first.

sections.title: The UTF8=ACCEPT Capability and Quoted-Strings
sections.content:
The UTF8=ACCEPT capability says the server can open mailboxes holding internationalized messages with SELECT and EXAMINE, and can give UTF-8 responses to LIST and LSUB. It also affects other extensions that return mailbox names, such as NAMESPACE and ACL. A client MUST use ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT to say it accepts UTF-8 in quoted-strings. That command is only valid in the authenticated state, and the server MUST NOT send UTF-8 in quoted-strings until the client has sent it.

IMAP4rev1 forbids 8-bit characters in atoms and quoted-strings, so UTF-8 could previously only travel as a literal, which costs an extra round trip per string unless the server offers non-synchronizing literals. With UTF8=ACCEPT, quoted-strings may contain UTF-8 characters (uQUOTED-CHAR). The server MUST reject, with a BAD response, any high-bit octet sequence that is not valid UTF-8.

Servers that support UTF8=ACCEPT SHOULD accept UTF-8 in mailbox names. Those that also support the mailbox international naming convention of RFC 3501 MUST accept UTF-8 and convert it to their internal format. Mailbox names MUST follow the Net-Unicode definition but MUST NOT contain control characters, the delete character, a line separator or a paragraph separator.

After enabling UTF-8, a client MUST NOT issue a SEARCH command that contains a charset specification, and a server SHOULD reject one with BAD. For commands with a mandatory charset field, such as SORT and THREAD, servers SHOULD reject charsets other than UTF-8 with BAD.
sections.eli5: Before using fancy letters, the mail program has to say 'I can read these.' Only after that does the server start sending them, and it rejects anything that is not proper UTF-8.

sections.title: APPEND, LOGIN and BODYSTRUCTURE
sections.content:
If the server supports UTF8=ACCEPT, APPEND accepts UTF-8 headers in the message argument. If the client has not issued ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT, the server MUST reject, with a NO response, an APPEND that has any 8-bit character in the message header fields.

The LOGIN command is not extended. A client that needs a UTF-8 username or password MUST use AUTHENTICATE, which can already carry them. Even then, whether such identities are allowed depends on the user provisioning system the server uses.

For FETCH BODYSTRUCTURE, RFC 9051 treats message/global like message/rfc822, so the response varies between IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2. This RFC extends the media-message syntax to match RFC 9051. With IMAP4rev1 and UTF8=ACCEPT enabled, the server MAY treat message/global like message/rfc822 or as RFC 3501 describes, and clients MUST accept both. With IMAP4rev2 the server MUST behave as RFC 9051 describes.
sections.eli5: Uploading a message with fancy letters only works if the client opted in. Passwords with fancy letters must use the special sign-in route, because the plain one was left alone.

sections.title: UTF8=ONLY and Legacy Clients
sections.content:
The UTF8=ONLY capability means the server supports UTF8=ACCEPT and also requires UTF-8 support from clients. The server will send UTF-8 in quoted-strings and will not accept the older modified UTF-7 mailbox naming. Because these changes are incompatible, a client MUST use ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT first, and a server advertising UTF8=ONLY rejects any command that might need UTF-8 and is not preceded by it, with NO [CANNOT]. A server advertises at most one of the two capabilities, and the client always sends ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT, never ENABLE UTF8=ONLY.

Servers will mostly have to cope with clients that do not enable UTF-8. The RFC says there is no completely satisfactory way to do that. Choices include hiding the problem messages, giving notifications or errors, or creating a surrogate of the message. Surrogates cannot truly substitute for the original: they are hard to reply to, and digital signatures over the original will often fail on them. Implementations that downgrade SHOULD use one of the algorithms in RFC 6857 or RFC 6858.

Servers also need extreme care with UIDVALIDITY when one user reaches the same mail by different clients or protocols. A client upgraded from not being UTF8=ACCEPT-aware MUST discard its cache of messages downloaded from the server. The RFC's advice for all cases is to upgrade legacy clients as soon as possible.
sections.eli5: Some servers say 'only fancy-letter mail programs allowed.' Servers that still serve old programs have to hide or simplify messages for them, and that is messy, so the best fix is updating the old programs.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of UTF-8 (RFC 3629) and of the PRECIS rules for usernames and passwords (RFC 8265) apply, particularly for UTF-8 in usernames and passwords. Otherwise the RFC is not believed to alter the security considerations of IMAP. The special cases arise when a non-conforming client accesses a conforming server, or when one message is reached by multiple clients using different protocols or capabilities, as discussed in Section 8.

For IANA, the "IMAP Capabilities" registry held references to RFC 6855. IANA updated them to point to this document. They cover UTF8=ACCEPT, UTF8=ONLY, and the obsolete UTF8=ALL, UTF8=APPEND and UTF8=USER.
sections.eli5: The main risks come from mixing old and new programs. Otherwise the safety rules stay the same, plus the usual care with fancy-letter usernames and passwords.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 6855
sections.content:
The document says it is an almost unchanged copy of RFC 6855 with two substantive changes. First, it removes the UTF8 data item of APPEND, so the syntax matches IMAP4rev2 and clients can support both versions with the same code. The RFC explains that no way exists to learn whether a message was stored with that data item. In July 2023 one of the authors found only one IMAP client using it, and that client used it incorrectly.

Second, it makes the message/global body structure syntax optional, since IMAP4rev1 and IMAP4rev2 differ slightly and storing a BODYSTRUCTURE the usual way could cause problems. Clients must parse both forms, which they need to do anyway to support both versions. The design rationale also says UTF8=ONLY was chosen over a 'just-send-UTF-8' approach because that one is hard to diagnose when it fails.
sections.eli5: This is a tidy-up edition. It removes a rarely and wrongly used feature and makes one rule flexible so servers are easier to build correctly.
